m1-s1.title: Declare a FastAPI application instance named 'app'.
m1-s1.summary: Import the FastAPI class and create an app instance to start building your API.
you_will_learn: Import FastAPI from the fastapi package
Instantiate the FastAPI class with parentheses
Assign the new instance to a variable named app

blocks.heading: Create Your FastAPI App Instance
blocks.body: First, import the `FastAPI` class from the `fastapi` package. Then, call it like any other Python class by adding parentheses `()` to create an instance. Finally, assign this new object to a variable, typically named `app`, which acts as your main application container.

items.title: Import the Class
items.text: Use `from fastapi import FastAPI` to bring the class into your current file.

items.title: Instantiate the App
items.text: Call `FastAPI()` with empty parentheses to create a new application instance.

items.title: Assign to Variable
items.text: Store the result in a variable like `app = FastAPI()` to use it for your routes.

blocks.title: Basic App Setup

blocks.text: The `app` variable is the main point of interaction to create all your API routes and logic.

m1-s2.title: Define a path operation decorator for a GET request at the root path.
m1-s2.summary: Learn how to add a GET route to your FastAPI app using the path operation decorator.
you_will_learn: Use @app.get() for GET routes
Specify path and HTTP method
Define the handler function

blocks.heading: Adding a GET Route with a Decorator
blocks.body: To handle requests, use the `@app.get()` decorator above your function. The first argument is the path (e.g., "/"). This tells FastAPI which URL and HTTP method to match.

items.title: Decorator Syntax
items.text: Place `@app.get("path")` directly above your function definition.

items.title: Path and Method
items.text: The string inside parentheses defines the URL path, while `get` sets the HTTP method.

blocks.title: Root GET Endpoint

blocks.text: You can use other methods like `@app.post()`, `@app.put()`, or `@app.delete()` for different HTTP verbs.

instructions: Import FastAPI from the fastapi package.
Initialize an instance of the FastAPI application.
Define a function named 'read_root' that returns a dictionary with status 'ok'.
Add the @app.get('/') decorator above the read_root function.

files.main.py:
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

hints: Use the @app.get() decorator to define a new route.
Place the decorator immediately above your function definition.
exercise.explanation: The reference implementation uses @app.get('/') to map the root path to the read_root function. The function returns a JSON object with 'status': 'ok'. Without this decorator, FastAPI would return a 404 Not Found for GET requests at '/', failing the evaluation cases.

m1-s3.title: Write an async function that returns a JSON dictionary when called.
m1-s3.summary: Learn to define an async function and return a JSON dictionary in FastAPI.
you_will_learn: Use async def for asynchronous functions
Return a dict to get JSON response

blocks.heading: Async Functions and JSON Responses
blocks.body: To make a function asynchronous, use the keyword `async` before `def`. To return JSON-compatible data, simply return a Python dictionary. FastAPI automatically converts this dictionary into a JSON response for you.

items.title: Async Keyword
items.text: Use `async def` to define an asynchronous function that can await tasks.

items.title: Return Dict
items.text: Returning a standard Python dictionary automatically results in a JSON response.

items.title: Auto-Conversion
items.text: FastAPI handles the conversion of your returned dict to JSON without extra code.

blocks.title: Simple Async Root Endpoint

blocks.text: You can also use a normal `def` instead of `async def`, but `async def` is required if you need to await something inside the function.

exercise.title: Async Function Returning JSON Dictionary

The outer function calls asyncio.run() to execute the async task synchronously for testing purposes. m2-s1.title: Define a FastAPI route that accepts a path parameter with a specific Python type annotation and returns that value in the JSON response.

blocks.heading: Path Parameter Types and Conversion
blocks.body: Declare the type of a path parameter directly in your function signature using standard Python type annotations. FastAPI automatically parses the URL string into the declared type (e.g., converting '3' to integer 3). If the input cannot be converted, FastAPI returns a validation error.

items.title: Type Annotations
items.text: Add a type like `int` or `str` after the parameter name in your function definition.

items.title: Automatic Conversion
items.text: FastAPI converts the URL string to the declared Python type before passing it to your function.

items.title: Validation Errors
items.text: If the input cannot be converted, FastAPI returns a 422 error with parsing details.

blocks.title: Integer Path Parameter Example

exercise.title: Echo an integer path parameter

m3-s1.title: Define a FastAPI endpoint that accepts optional query parameters with default values and returns different responses based on their presence.
m3-s1.summary: Learn how to declare optional query parameters with default values in FastAPI endpoints.
you_will_learn: Set default values for query parameters

blocks.heading: Optional Query Parameters with Defaults
blocks.body: To declare an optional query parameter, set its default value to `None`. FastAPI recognizes non-path parameters as query parameters. If a user does not provide the parameter in the URL, it defaults to `None` inside your function. You can then check if the value exists (e.g., using `if q:`) to return different responses.

items.title: Declare Optional Parameters
items.text: Set the default value of a query parameter to `None` to make it optional in your FastAPI endpoint.

items.title: Default Behavior
items.text: When a query parameter is omitted from the URL, FastAPI passes its default value (e.g., `None`) to your function automatically.

items.title: Conditional Logic
items.text: Use conditional checks like `if q:` inside your handler to distinguish between provided values and the default `None` state.

blocks.title: Optional Query Parameter Example

blocks.text: FastAPI determines a parameter is optional because of the default value `= None`, not just the type annotation `str | None`.

docs.label: `Query` as the default value or in `Annotated`
Query parameter list / multiple values with defaults

blocks.heading: Boolean Query Parameters
blocks.body: Declare a boolean query parameter by annotating the function argument with `bool`. FastAPI automatically converts common string representations like 'true', '1', or 'on' to Python `True`, and 'false', '0', or 'off' to `False`. If you omit the parameter in the URL, FastAPI uses your specified default value.

items.title: Type Annotation
items.text: Annotate the function argument with `bool` to enable automatic string-to-boolean conversion.

items.title: Default Value
items.text: Set a default value like `False` so the parameter is optional and handles missing inputs gracefully.

items.title: Conversion Rules
items.text: FastAPI converts 'true', '1', 'on' to True, while 'false', '0', 'off' convert to False.

blocks.title: Boolean Query Parameter Example

blocks.text: If you omit the `short` parameter in the URL, FastAPI uses the default value `False`. An empty value like `?short=` causes a validation error.

m3-s4.title: Implement a POST endpoint that accepts both path parameters and a request body containing a Pydantic model.
m3-s4.summary: Learn how to declare function parameters for path and request body data in FastAPI.
you_will_learn: Declare Pydantic models as request body parameters
Use type annotations for path parameters
Distinguish between path, query, and body sources
Handle multiple parameter types in one route

blocks.heading: Mixing Path Parameters and Request Bodies
blocks.body: To receive data from the request body, declare a function parameter as a Pydantic model (e.g., `item: Item`). FastAPI distinguishes sources by type: parameters matching path syntax like `{item_id}` are taken from the URL path. Singular types like `int` or `str` without default values are treated as query parameters. Pydantic models are always taken from the request body.

items.title: Path Parameters
items.text: Parameters matching the URL pattern (e.g., `{item_id}`) are extracted from the path and passed to the function.

items.title: Request Body
items.text: Parameters declared as Pydantic models (e.g., `item: Item`) are automatically read from the request body.

items.title: Query Parameters
items.text: Singular types like `int` or `str` without defaults are interpreted as query parameters unless they match a path variable.

blocks.title: Update Item with Path and Body

blocks.text: FastAPI allows multiple body parameters in a function, but only one will be populated from the actual request body.

blocks.heading: Using Field for Model Validation
blocks.body: Import `Field` from `pydantic`, not `fastapi`. Use it inside Pydantic models to set defaults, titles, or constraints like `max_length` or `gt`. You can mix Path, Query, and Body parameters in a single endpoint. FastAPI recognizes types automatically: path params use `{}`, query params are singular types with defaults, and Pydantic models become the request body.

items.title: Import Field from pydantic
items.text: Always import `Field` from `pydantic`, not `fastapi`. It works like `Query` or `Body` but for model attributes.

items.title: Add constraints to fields
items.text: Use `Field(gt=0, max_length=300)` to enforce rules like positive numbers or string length limits.

items.title: Mix parameter types freely
items.text: Combine Path, Query, and Body parameters in one route; FastAPI handles each source correctly.

blocks.title: Mixed Parameters with Field Validation

blocks.text: Remember: `Field` is from `pydantic`, while `Path`, `Query`, and `Body` are from `fastapi`. Don't mix them up!

m4-s2.title: Define nested models where attributes are lists or sets of submodels with type parameters.
m4-s2.summary: Learn to define Pydantic models with attributes that are lists or sets of submodels using standard Python type syntax.
you_will_learn: Declare a list of strings with square brackets
Define a set of unique items using the set type
Use a Pydantic model as an element in a list
Understand how FastAPI handles nested JSON structures

blocks.heading: Defining Lists and Sets in Pydantic Models
blocks.body: To define a list or set attribute in a Pydantic model, use standard Python type syntax with square brackets. For example, `list[str]` declares a list of strings, while `set[str]` declares a set of unique strings. You can also nest Pydantic models inside these lists, like `list[Image]`, to accept JSON arrays containing objects.

items.title: List Type Syntax
items.text: Use square brackets with the internal type, such as `list[str]` or `list[Image]`, to declare a list of specific elements.

items.title: Set Type Syntax
items.text: Declare unique items using `set[str]`. FastAPI will automatically convert duplicate inputs into a set of unique values.

items.title: Nested Models
items.text: You can use Pydantic models as subtypes inside lists, allowing you to validate complex nested JSON structures.

blocks.title: Item Model with List and Set Attributes
blocks.code:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Image(BaseModel):
    url: str
    name: str

class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    tags: set[str] = set()
    images: list[Image] | None = None

blocks.text: If you forget to use a `set` and use a `list` instead, FastAPI will still convert it to a `set` if your model definition expects a `set`.

docs.label: Declare a `list` with a type parameter

m4-s3.title: Create separate input and output Pydantic models to filter sensitive data like passwords from the response.
m4-s3.summary: Create separate Pydantic models to filter sensitive fields like passwords from API responses using response_model.
you_will_learn: Define input and output Pydantic models
Annotate routes with different models for filtering
Use response_model_exclude_unset to omit default values

blocks.heading: Filtering Sensitive Data with Separate Models
blocks.body: To hide sensitive data like passwords, define an input model (e.g., UserIn) that includes them and an output model (e.g., UserOut) that excludes them. Annotate your route's `response_model` parameter with the output model. FastAPI will automatically filter the response to match the output model, even if your function returns the full input object.

items.title: Define Separate Models
items.text: Create a Pydantic model without sensitive fields and use it as the `response_model` parameter in your route decorator.

items.title: Annotate with Output Model
items.text: Set the `response_model` parameter on the decorator to tell FastAPI which fields should appear in the JSON response.

items.title: Exclude Unset Values
items.text: Use `response_model_exclude_unset=True` to ensure only explicitly set values are included, omitting default field values.

blocks.title: Creating a User with Hidden Password
blocks.code:
from typing import Any

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr

app = FastAPI()

class UserIn(BaseModel):
    username: str
    password: str
    email: EmailStr
    full_name: str | None = None

class UserOut(BaseModel):
    username: str
    email: EmailStr
    full_name: str | None = None

@app.post("/user/", response_model=UserOut)
async def create_user(user: UserIn) -> Any:
    return user

blocks.text: If you use `response_model_exclude_unset=True`, default values like empty lists or zero floats will not appear in the JSON response.

m4-s4.title: Configure a response to return a Union of multiple types or an arbitrary dict with typed keys and values.
m4-s4.summary: Learn to declare FastAPI responses as a Union of models or an arbitrary dict with typed keys and values.
you_will_learn: Use typing.Union for multiple response types
Declare dict[str, float] for weighted keywords
Apply response_model parameter for validation
Understand OpenAPI anyOf generation

blocks.heading: Flexible Response Types: Unions and Arbitrary Dicts
blocks.body: FastAPI allows flexible responses using `typing.Union` or the `response_model` parameter. For a Union, place specific types first (e.g., `PlaneItem | CarItem`). For arbitrary dicts, use `dict[str, float]`. You can also use `response_model=dict[str, float]` to validate dict keys/values without defining a Pydantic model.

items.title: Union Syntax
items.text: Use `typing.Union[A, B]` or the pipe operator `A | B`. Order matters: put specific types before general ones.

items.title: Arbitrary Dicts
items.text: Annotate with `dict[str, float]` to accept JSON objects where keys are strings and values are floats.

items.title: Validation Priority
items.text: The `response_model` parameter overrides the return type annotation for OpenAPI schema and validation logic.

blocks.title: Union Response with Car or Plane

blocks.text: If you declare both a return type and `response_model`, FastAPI uses `response_model` for validation and OpenAPI schema.

blocks.heading: Raising Custom HTTP Errors
blocks.body: To return a structured error, import `HTTPException` from `fastapi`. Inside your endpoint logic, use `raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="...", headers={"X-Custom": "value"})`. This stops execution immediately and sends the defined status code, message, and headers to the client.

items.title: Importing the Exception
items.text: Use `from fastapi import HTTPException` to access the error class in your imports.

items.title: Passing Arguments
items.text: Provide `status_code`, `detail`, and optional `headers` when raising the exception.

items.title: Execution Stops
items.text: Raising an exception terminates the request immediately without running remaining code in the function.

blocks.title: Endpoint with Custom Headers

blocks.text: Remember that `HTTPException` inherits from Starlette's version; register handlers for Starlette's class if you need to catch internal errors.

m5-s2.title: Define a dependency function that accepts query parameters and returns a dictionary of values.
m5-s2.summary: Learn to declare dependencies with query parameters using Annotated and Depends.
you_will_learn: Declare a dependency function returning a dict
Use Annotated to combine type hints with Depends
Reuse dependency definitions across multiple routes

blocks.heading: Declaring Dependencies with Query Parameters
blocks.body: A dependency is a callable function that FastAPI executes before your endpoint. Use `Depends()` to link it to an endpoint parameter. Wrap the return type in `Annotated` to tell FastAPI how to handle the result. You can define the dependency once and reuse it.

items.title: Define a Dependency Function
items.text: Create an async function that accepts query parameters like `q`, `skip`, and `limit`, returning a dictionary.

items.title: Use Annotated with Depends
items.text: Combine the return type hint with `Depends()` inside `Annotated` to declare the dependency parameter in your endpoint.

items.title: Reuse Dependency Definitions
items.text: Store the `Annotated` definition in a variable or alias and use it across multiple endpoints to avoid duplication.

blocks.title: Reusable Dependency with Query Parameters
blocks.code:
from typing import Annotated

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

async def common_parameters(q: str | None = None, skip: int = 0, limit: int = 100):
    return {"q": q, "skip": skip, "limit": limit}

CommonsDep = Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]

@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(commons: CommonsDep):
    return commons

@app.get("/users/")
async def read_users(commons: CommonsDep):
    return commons

blocks.text: FastAPI calls your dependency function automatically. Do not call it manually with parentheses in the endpoint signature.

m5-s3.title: Create a class that acts as a dependency by implementing __init__ and using it with Depends().
m5-s3.summary: Learn how to define callable class dependencies and use Annotated with them in FastAPI.
you_will_learn: Define a Python class as a dependency
Use Annotated with a class type
Pass the class directly to Depends

blocks.heading: Callable Class Dependencies
blocks.body: A dependency in FastAPI must be callable. A Python class is callable because you call it to create an instance (e.g., `Cat()`). You can use a class as a dependency by passing the class itself to `Depends`. FastAPI will then call the class (using its `__init__`) to get the values for your endpoint.

items.title: Class Callability
items.text: FastAPI treats any callable object as a dependency, including classes that define an `__init__` method.

items.title: Using Annotated with Classes
items.text: Wrap the class type in `Annotated` and pass the class itself to `Depends` inside the route function parameter.

items.title: Parameter Extraction
items.text: FastAPI extracts arguments from the class's `__init__` signature just like it does for functions.

blocks.title: Class Dependency Example
blocks.code:
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

class CommonQueryParams:
    def __init__(self, q: str | None = None, skip: int = 0, limit: int = 100):
        self.q = q
        self.skip = skip
        self.limit = limit

fake_items_db = [{"item_name": "Foo"}, {"item_name": "Bar"}, {"item_name": "Baz"}]

@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(commons: Annotated[CommonQueryParams, Depends(CommonQueryParams)]):
    response = {}
    if commons.q:
        response.update({"q": commons.q})
    items = fake_items_db[commons.skip : commons.skip + commons.limit]
    response.update({"items": items})
    return response

blocks.text: Prefer using `Annotated` with the class type instead of non-Annotated versions for better tooling support.
